title: Domain and Range for All Four Section 3.7 Functions
subtitle: Unit 3 • Lecture 45 • Section 3.7 Domain & Range
detail: State domain and range for all four graphed parabolas.
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
solution:
| Function | Domain | Range |
|---|---|---|
| $g(x)=x^2+6x+5$ | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $[-4,\infty)$ |
| $h(x)=-2x^2+4x+6$ | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $(-\infty,8]$ |
| $g(x)=2x^2-8x$ | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $[-8,\infty)$ |
| $f(x)=-\frac{1}{2}(x+1)^2+8$ | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $(-\infty,8]$ |

**Rule:** Domain is ALWAYS $(-\infty,\infty)$ for quadratic functions. Range depends on direction (up/down) and vertex y-value.
pitfall: **Sora’s Memory Trick:** Opens UP → Range has a minimum $[k, \infty)$. Opens DOWN → Range has a maximum $(-\infty, k]$.
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 2 reviews Domain and Range across all four Section 3.7 functions from our workbook.

[TA Sora] Function 1: $g(x) = x^2 + 6x + 5$. Vertex is $(-3, -4)$, and it opens upward. Domain is $(-\infty, \infty)$ and Range is $[-4, \infty)$!

[Prof. Park] Function 2: $h(x) = -2x^2 + 4x + 6$. Vertex is $(1, 8)$, and it opens downward because $a = -2 < 0$. Range is $(-\infty, 8]$!

[TA Sora] Function 3: $g(x) = 2x^2 - 8x$. Vertex is $(2, -8)$, opens upward. Range is $[-8, \infty)$!

[Prof. Park] Function 4: $f(x) = -\frac{1}{2}(x + 1)^2 + 8$. Vertex is $(-1, 8)$, opens downward. Range is $(-\infty, 8]$!

[TA Sora] Notice the universal rule: Domain of EVERY quadratic function is $(-\infty, \infty)$. Range always starts or ends at the vertex $y$-value $k$!

title: Full Graph: $ p(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5 $ — 5-Point Method
subtitle: Unit 3 • Lecture 45 • Comprehensive Graphing Practice
detail: Apply the complete 5-point method from scratch.
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Graph $p(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5$ using the 5-point method:**

**Step 1 — Vertex:**
$$x = \dfrac{-(-4)}{2(1)} = \dfrac{4}{2} = 2$$
$$p(2) = 4-8-5 = -9$$
**Vertex:** $(2,\,-9)$ — Minimum

**Step 2 — y-intercept:**
$$p(0) = -5 \Rightarrow (0,\,-5)$$
solution:
**Step 3 — x-intercepts:** Set $p(x)=0$
$$x^2-4x-5=0 \Rightarrow (x-5)(x+1)=0$$
$$x = 5 \quad \text{or} \quad x=-1$$
**x-intercepts:** $(-1,0)$ and $(5,0)$

**Step 4 — Symmetric point** of $(0,-5)$:
Axis of symmetry: $x=2$. Distance from 0 to 2 is 2. Mirror: $x=4$
$$p(4) = 16-16-5 = -5 \Rightarrow (4,\,-5)\text{ \checkmark}$$

**Step 5 — Five key points:**
$(-1,0)$, $(0,-5)$, $(2,-9)$, $(4,-5)$, $(5,0)$

**Domain:** $(-\infty,\infty)$ \qquad **Range:** $[-9,\infty)$
pitfall: **Sora’s Check:** Verify the symmetric point by computing $p(4)$ directly. It should equal $p(0) = -5$. \checkmark Symmetry confirmed!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 3 summarizes our 5-Point Graphing Masterclass: 1. Vertex $(h, k)$, 2. $y$-intercept $(0, c)$, 3. Symmetric reflection of the $y$-intercept, 4 & 5. The two $x$-intercepts (or test points if roots are imaginary).

[TA Sora] Remember to always sketch the Axis of Symmetry $x = h$ as a dashed line. It acts as your visual mirror, ensuring that both wings of the parabola open with identical curvature and width.

[Prof. Park] A 5-point parabola is a piece of mathematical art. You have mastered this craft!

[Prof. Park] On slide 3, let's execute the full 5-Point Graphing Method on p(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5: 1. a = 1 > 0: opens upward. 2. Vertex x = -(-4) / (2 ÃÂ· 1) = 4 / 2 = 2. p(2) = 2^2 - 4(2) - 5 = 4 - 8 - 5 = -9. Vertex is (2, -9)! 3. Axis of symmetry: x = 2. 4. y-intercept: (0, -5). Its reflection across x = 2 is (4, -5)! 5. x-intercepts: (x - 5)(x + 1) = 0 -> (5, 0) and (-1, 0). Look at our five points: (-1, 0), (0, -5), (2, -9), (4, -5), (5, 0). They form a gorgeously symmetric parabola with domain (-infinity, infinity) and range [-9, infinity)!

[TA Sora] In p(x) = x^2 - 4x - 5, notice how the axis of symmetry x = 2 creates symmetric point pairs: x = 1 and x = 3 are both 1 unit away from the axis: p(1) = 1 - 4 - 5 = -8, and p(3) = 9 - 12 - 5 = -8! Identical! x = 0 and x = 4 are both 2 units away: p(0) = -5, and p(4) = 16 - 16 - 5 = -5! Identical! x = -1 and x = 5 are both 3 units away: p(-1) = 0, and p(5) = 0! Identical! Symmetry is your greatest friend when graphing parabolas: compute one side, and you get the other side for free!

slideTypeLabel: Parabola vs. Line on Same Graph
title: Intersection of $ f(x) = x^2-6x+4 $ and $ g(x) = -2x+25 $
subtitle: Unit 3 • Lecture 45 • Section 3.7 Example 5F Visual (Workbook p. 89)
detail: Graph both functions and identify their intersection points.
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Graph both $f(x) = x^2-6x+4$ (parabola) and $g(x) = -2x+25$ (line) on the same axes.**

**Parabola $f(x)$:**
- Vertex: $x=3$, $f(3)=9-18+4=-5$ → $(3,-5)$
- y-intercept: $(0,4)$
- x-intercepts: $x^2-6x+4=0$ → $x=3\pm\sqrt{5}\approx(5.24,0)$ and $(0.76,0)$

**Line $g(x)$:**
- y-intercept: $(0,25)$
- x-intercept: $-2x+25=0$ → $x=12.5$
solution:
**Intersection (from Lecture 44, Part F):**
$$f(x) = g(x) \Rightarrow x^2-4x-21=0 \Rightarrow (x-7)(x+3)=0$$
$$x = 7 \quad \text{or} \quad x=-3$$

**Intersection points:**
- At $x=7$: $g(7) = -14+25 = 11$ → $(7,\,11)$
- At $x=-3$: $g(-3) = 6+25 = 31$ → $(-3,\,31)$

**Visual:** The line $g$ crosses the parabola $f$ at $(-3,31)$ and $(7,11)$. Between these points, the line is above the parabola.
pitfall: **Sora’s Observation:** Where $g(x) > f(x)$, the line is above the parabola. Where $g(x) < f(x)$, the parabola is above the line. The intersection points are the switchover!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 4 connects quadratics to real-world physics: projectile motion $h(t) = -16t^2 + v_0 t + h_0$, where $-16$ represents half the acceleration of gravity in feet per second squared!

[TA Sora] Look at how our algebraic tools answer real questions: 1. The $y$-intercept $h_0$ is the initial launch height! 2. The vertex formula $t = -v_0 / (2a)$ gives the exact time of maximum altitude! 3. The vertex height $k$ is the maximum altitude reached! 4. The positive $x$-intercept where $h(t) = 0$ is the exact moment of splashdown or ground impact!

[Prof. Park] Whether tracking a golf ball, an arrow, a wildfire retardant drop from an aircraft in Montana, or an artillery trajectory, quadratic functions govern physical flight.

[TA Sora] Algebra is the operating system of the physical world!

[TA Sora] On slide 4, visualizing the intersection of f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 4 and g(x) = -2x + 25: A line and a parabola can interact in three distinct geometric ways: They can miss each other entirely (0 intersection points, Delta < 0). The line can graze the parabola tangentially (1 intersection point, Delta = 0). Or the line can cut through both branches (2 intersection points, Delta > 0). Here, our system had Delta = (-4)^2 - 4(1)(-21) = 16 + 84 = 100 > 0, producing two real intersection coordinates: (-3, 31) and (7, 11)!

[Prof. Park] Think of this system of equations in real Montana civil engineering: The parabola f(x) represents a cross-section of a mountain valley, and the line g(x) represents the grade of an elevated highway bridge spanning the canyon. The intersection points (7, 11) and (-3, 31) are the exact bridge abutment coordinates where the highway bridge anchors into the solid bedrock of the mountain! Algebra is the language that builds real, safe physical infrastructure.

[TA Sora] You have built a powerhouse foundation that will carry you through college algebra, precalculus, and beyond! Be proud of your hard work and keep that momentum going strong!

title: Unit 3 Grand Review: All Methods for Quadratic Functions
subtitle: Unit 3 • Lecture 45 • Complete Unit Summary
detail: Comprehensive review of all Unit 3 concepts.
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Unit 3 — All Methods Mastered:**

| Section | Topic | Method |
|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | Quadratic Functions intro | Identify vertex, direction |
| 3.1 | Vertex & y-intercept | $x=-b/2a$, plug in |
| 3.2 | x-intercepts | Square Root Property |
| 3.3 | x-intercepts | Factoring |
| 3.4 | x-intercepts | Completing the Square |
| 3.5 | x-intercepts | Quadratic Formula $\pm\sqrt{\Delta}$ |
| 3.6 | Mixed methods | Choose best approach |
| 3.7 | Full graph | 5-point method + Domain/Range |
solution:
**The Master Decision Tree:**
1. Is it in vertex form $a(x-h)^2+k$? → Read vertex directly
2. No $b$ term? → Square Root Property
3. No $c$ term? → Factor out GCF
4. Factors nicely? → Factor
5. Otherwise → **Quadratic Formula** (always works!)

**5-Point Graph Checklist:**
$\square$ Vertex $\square$ y-intercept $\square$ x-intercept(s) $\square$ Symmetric point $\square$ Smooth curve
pitfall: **Sora’s Final Wisdom:** When in doubt, use the Quadratic Formula. It ALWAYS works and never fails. But always set the equation to zero first!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 5 presents the Grand Review of all four quadratic solving methods: 1. Square Root Property ($X^2 = k$), 2. Factoring ($(x - r_1)(x - r_2) = 0$), 3. Completing the Square ($(x + b/2)^2 = k$), and 4. The Quadratic Formula ($x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$).

[TA Sora] You now command all four methods. You know when to deploy each tool for maximum speed, accuracy, and elegance.

[Prof. Park] No quadratic equation can intimidate you ever again!

[Prof. Park] Look at our Unit 3 Grand Review table on slide 5: In Section 3.0, we explored the geometry of parabolas. In Section 3.1 and 3.2, we mastered the Vertex Formula x = -b/(2a) and standard form. In Section 3.3, we solved equations and found intercepts by Factoring. In Section 3.4, we completed the square and built vertex form. In Section 3.5, we mastered the Quadratic Formula and the Discriminant. In Section 3.6, we learned how to choose the best method for any problem. And in Section 3.7, we mastered full 5-point graphing and system intersections!

[TA Sora] Let's do a fast recap of how all the pieces of Unit 3 connect: Every single quadratic function has a vertex that marks its maximum or minimum. Every quadratic function has an axis of symmetry passing through that vertex. Its y-intercept is always (0, c). Its x-intercepts are found by setting f(x) = 0 and choosing the best of our four methods. And its graph is a smooth, continuous U-shaped curve with infinite domain.

title: Challenge: Complete Analysis of $ q(x) = -3x^2 + 12x - 9 $
subtitle: Unit 3 • Lecture 45 • Final Challenge
detail: Find all features and graph this quadratic completely.
instructor: Prof. Eunju Park • TA Sora (Gallatin College MSU)
problem:
**Find all features and graph $q(x) = -3x^2 + 12x - 9$:**

1. Direction of opening
2. Vertex
3. Axis of symmetry
4. y-intercept
5. x-intercept(s) — use best method
6. Domain and Range
solution:
**1. Direction:** $a=-3<0$ → Opens **downward** (maximum)

**2. Vertex:** $x=\dfrac{-12}{2(-3)}=\dfrac{-12}{-6}=2$
$$q(2)=-3(4)+12(2)-9=-12+24-9=\mathbf{3}$$
**Vertex: $(2,3)$**

**3. Axis of Symmetry:** $x=2$

**4. y-intercept:** $q(0)=-9$ → $(0,-9)$

**5. x-intercepts:** Factor out $-3$:
$$-3x^2+12x-9=0 \Rightarrow x^2-4x+3=0 \Rightarrow (x-1)(x-3)=0$$
$$x=1 \text{ or } x=3$$
**x-intercepts: $(1,0)$ and $(3,0)$**

**6. Domain:** $(-\infty,\infty)$ \quad **Range:** $(-\infty,3]$
pitfall: **Sora’s Shortcut:** Divide by $-3$ first: $x^2-4x+3=0$ is much easier to factor than $-3x^2+12x-9=0$!
script:
[Prof. Park] Slide 7 provides final mastery problem solving and reflection on personal growth, persistence, and logical reasoning.

[TA Sora] Remember where you started in Lecture 1. You may have felt hesitant or anxious about algebra. But you showed up, you practiced on paper, you embraced protective parentheses, and you conquered every challenge step by step!

[Prof. Park] That persistence is the greatest skill you take from this class. Math teaches us that no problem is permanentÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂwith the right tools, structure, and patience, every problem can be solved.

[Prof. Park] In Challenge Problem q(x) = -3x^2 + 12x - 9: a = -3 (opens down). Vertex x = -12 / (2 ÃÂ· -3) = -12 / -6 = 2. q(2) = -3(4) + 12(2) - 9 = -12 + 24 - 9 = +3. Vertex is (2, 3)! Factor: -3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = -3(x - 3)(x - 1) = 0 -> intercepts (1, 0) and (3, 0). y-intercept: (0, -9). Symmetric point: (4, -9). Domain: (-infinity, infinity). Range: (-infinity, 3]! Complete, elegant, and fully verified.

[TA Sora] In our final Challenge Problem q(x) = -3x^2 + 12x - 9: Notice that factoring out -3 gave -3(x^2 - 4x + 3) = -3(x - 3)(x - 1) = 0. The intercepts are (1, 0) and (3, 0). Halfway between 1 and 3 is x = 2! And plugging in x = 2 gave q(2) = 3: the vertex is (2, 3)! The vertex x-coordinate is ALWAYS the exact midpoint of the x-intercepts! Midpoint: (1 + 3) / 2 = 2. It all fits together into one cohesive, harmonious system!
